rss_0_1791244417.title: The top cancer success stories of the past 50 years, by the numbers
rss_0_1791244417.text:
Improvements in cancer treatment in the past half-century have made many forms of the condition less deadly.Credit: Doaa Albaz/Middle East Images/AFP/Getty

An analysis showcases the past half-century’s biggest cancer success stories — but also highlights the recalcitrant malignancies that continue to vex researchers.

The report, released last month by the American Association for Cancer Research1 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, finds that 71% of people with cancer in the United States will live for at least five years after diagnosis, up from 49% in the late 1970s (see ‘Uneven progress’).

Among the success stories, gains in lung cancer survival rates are particularly striking, says Rebecca Siegel, a cancer epidemiologist at the American Cancer Society in Atlanta, Georgia. Lung cancer is one of the world’s biggest causes of death, and on average, only 13% of people diagnosed with lung cancer between 1975 and 1979 lived for another five years. Between 2016 and 2022, that number reached 29%. “It’s still really low, but it’s such an improvement,” says Siegel.

That jump in survival rates comes from improvements in surgical techniques and radiation treatments, as well as new medicines that either unleash the immune system against tumours or target cancer cells bearing specific mutations. “It’s very heartwarming,” says Michel Coleman, an epidemiologist at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine. Coleman says global statistics broadly exhibit this same trend towards greater survival.

Meanwhile, progress in treating childhood leukaemias is widely considered to be among the greatest achievements in cancer research. For children and adolescents up to 19 years old, the 5-year survival rate for lymphoid leukaemia has risen from 57% to 90%. That boost came not from the discovery of a transformative therapy, but from the careful, collaborative tweaking of dosages and timings for treatments that were already available, says Siegel.

Other highlights include liver cancer, for which five-year survival has tripled to 22% since the mid-1990s2, says Siegel. Survival rates for people with multiple myeloma, a type of blood cancer, have also increased drastically, in part owing to the development of drugs that harness the immune system.

Room for improvement

rss_1_1791244418.title: ‘What took them so long?’ This year’s medicine Nobel winner is overdue
rss_1_1791244418.text:
I’ve covered the Nobel prizes for Nature for the past 15 years — but there are so many potentially Nobel-worthy discoveries that as the awards near it can feel like a waste of time trying to anticipate just one or two.

Part of the reason I feel that way is illustrated by today’s winner of the Nobel prize in Physiology or Medicine, optogenetics. Its foundational work was done two decades ago, in the early 2000s, and the 2026 award honours three scientists: Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel. For years, as Nobel week approached, my colleague — who profiled Deisseroth for Nature in back in 2013 — and I would ponder if this was finally going to be the year for optogenetics, which has transformed how neuroscientists understand the brain.

It turns out I wasn’t alone. “We’ve been waiting for this for a long time,” Michael Häusser, a neuroscientist at Hong Kong University and University College London, told me this afternoon. “What took them so long?”

Häusser reminded me that optogenetics won its first major award, the Brain Prize, in 2013. Unlike the Nobel Prize, which is limited to three awardees, that award also recognized three other optogenetics pioneers: Edward Boyden, Gero Miesenböck and Ernst Bamburg.

Häusser thinks the Nobel Committee may have taken so long to recognize the field because the direct application of optogenetics to human disease and biology has emerged only in the past few years.

rss_2_1791244420.title: Medicine Nobel awarded for brain ‘switch’ that controls neurons with light
rss_2_1791244420.text:
Left to right: Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel were awarded the 2026 medicine Nobel on 5 October.Credit: L-R Stanford Medicine, Humbold-Universität zu Berlin/Philipp Plum, Robert Emmerich/Universität Würzburg

After being on many scientists’ shortlists for years, optogenetics — a technology that allows researchers to control the brain’s neurons with pulses of light — has been recognized by the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. The technique has transformed how neuroscientists study the brain, offering them a way to test cause and effect.

‘What took them so long?’ This year’s medicine Nobel winner is overdue

The winners are Karl Deisseroth at Stanford University in California, Peter Hegemann at the Humboldt University of Berlin and Georg Nagel at the University of Würzburg in Germany. They share the prize of 12 million Swedish kronor (US$1.2 million) equally.

Deisseroth said that, as a night owl, he had been working late before he received the call from the Nobel committee. “It was a complete surprise,” he told a press conference held by Stanford University today. “I was lying down, just starting to drift off to sleep, and my phone rang at my bedside,” he said. “There were about 30 seconds where I had trouble forming words … but [it’s] very exciting and overwhelming, and just delightful.”

A switch neuroscientists dreamt of

Neuroscientists’ aim is to unpick the brain’s many roles: how it governs feelings, behaviours and bodily functions. To understand how the brain works and how its cells mediate different behaviours, scientists require an approach that can perturb the system with high precision.

“Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” said Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine, in the press release announcing the prize.

Working together in the early 2000s, Hegemann and Nagel discovered a light-sensitive protein called channelrhodopsin1,2 in the alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, which is able to swim towards a light source. In response to blue light, the protein opens to allow charged molecules to flood into cells, creating a tiny electrical charge.

Can you name the women who have won a science Nobel prize?

In later work, Deisseroth and his colleagues inserted3 the gene encoding channelrhodopsin into neurons of rodents, and found that it caused the cells to fire and communicate with other neurons. The technology — a light-controlled ‘switch’ that allowed neuroscientists to alter specific cell types in the neural circuits of living brains using genetics — soon came to be known as optogenetics. It revolutionized neuroscience.

“We use light to turn on or off individual cells, or even types of cell or connections from one part of the brain to another. We can turn those on and off with millisecond precision in real time during behaviour, during cognition, and that allows us to see what actually matters for brain function and to start to map function and dysfunction precisely,” said Deisseroth. “It’s a real confluence of engineering and medicine.”

Illuminating the brain

The prizewinners’ work “fundamentally changed how we conduct neuroscience” and has “influenced fields far beyond it in biology, and opened new therapeutic possibilities,” says neuroscientist Rui Costa, who is president and chief executive of the Allen Institute in Seattle, Washington. “I first met Karl 23 years ago, and he was already thinking deeply about how to control the activity of specific neurons to understand and alter behaviour. Karl’s commitment not only to discovery, but also to sharing tools and reagents at scale, was equally transformative,” says Costa.

How to win a Nobel prize: what kind of scientist scoops medals?

The discovery and application of channelrhodopsin have led to a diverse ‘optogenetic toolkit’ that allows scientists in different fields to harness cellular activity with light.

Optogenetics has had a great impact on basic science, says Alexander Gottschalk, a neuroscientist at Goethe University Frankfurt in Germany. “It’s such an easy way, a very precise way, to define which cells should become responsive,” says Gottschalk. “Many people in the field have expected [this] for several rounds of Nobels already, but it took until now.”

Gottschalk has worked with all three winners, but knows Nagel the best. “He’s a humble person. He’s a modest person,” says Gottschalk. “I’m really happy that he received this prize today. It’s really well deserved.”

Into the clinic

Insights provided by optogenetic tools have helped researchers to better understand healthy brain function and conditions such as depression, schizophrenia, Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s.

rss_3_1791244424.title: How big tech is building a military–industrial complex in the age of AI
rss_3_1791244424.text:
Bytes and Bullets: Global Rivalries, Private Tech, and the Future of Modern Warfare Steve Feldstein Monoray (2026)

Valley of Death: How Big Tech is Fueling the Future of War Sharon Weinberger Little, Brown and Company (2026)

States have been competing to gain a technological advantage over others for millennia. More than 3,500 years ago, ancient Egyptians’ success in the race to mastering horse-drawn chariots helped them to dominate their region militarily. Today, a similar contest is under way as global powers vie for supremacy in artificial intelligence and technologies such as drones, space-based weapon systems and advanced semiconductors.

Two books examine this latest arms race and ask who might prevail. In Bytes and Bullets, former US state department official Steve Feldstein discusses how technological innovations are becoming “crucial pieces in a geopolitical chess match”. He examines cases including Israel’s early leadership in drone technology and the various innovative prototypes being tested on battlefields in Ukraine.

How AI is shaping the war in Iran — and what’s next for future conflicts

In Valley of Death, security-focused journalist Sharon Weinberger shares how technologies have been adopted by the US defence establishment. Rich in detail, her book takes readers inside the meetings, negotiations and contracting battles that have helped to make Silicon Valley an integral part of the US national-security apparatus.

Weinberger challenges the idea that Silicon Valley is inherently libertarian and instinctively hostile to government power. She shows instead how the Pentagon helped to nurture the early growth of many technology firms, how these companies amassed enough wealth and influence to operate independently of the state and how the defence establishment is now seeking to reforge ties with tech founders and investors who have greater autonomy than conventional military contractors ever did. She calls this evolving relationship the Pentagon–Silicon Complex.

For Weinberger, the nexus between government and tech industry is best illustrated by the story of NeXT, the computer company Steve Jobs founded after leaving Apple. She recounts how Pentagon funding helped to transform northern California into a hub for electronics and computing at the beginning of the cold war, and how that had started to change by the 1980s. Intelligence agencies increasingly looked to the private sector for technology that outperformed their own. The CIA, for example, turned to NeXT because its powerful and user-friendly computers were better suited to analysing and sharing satellite imagery than were the government systems. It wanted as many as 20,000 workstations, modified with faster processors and specialist graphics hardware.

Of spies and space

Those secretive government purchases provided a crucial lifeline for NeXT during its struggling early years, because the firm discovered that the university market it initially hoped to reach wouldn’t fund it. The government investments helped the company to survive long enough for Apple to acquire it for US$400 million in December 1996 and rehire Jobs. As Weinberger puts it, “The spies had saved Jobs.” Without the CIA’s support, she argues, the NeXT–Apple merger might never have happened. NeXT’s software became the foundation for the Mac operating system and, by extension, that of the iPhone, which is now used by hundreds of millions of people.

Weinberger then traces the shifts in the relationship between Silicon Valley and the US national-security establishment in subsequent decades. PayPal co-founder Peter Thiel and his Stanford Law School contemporary Alex Karp, for instance, adapted techniques they had developed at PayPal for detecting fraud to build the software firm Palantir, which they and others co-founded in 2003. Palantir’s platform could sift through vast quantities of intelligence data.

Elon Musk sells launch services for his commercial space rockets to the US government.Credit: Saul Martinez/Getty

Former PayPal chief executive Elon Musk develops rockets commercially at SpaceX, the space-technology firm he founded and sells launch services to the US government and military. This way, Musk retains ownership of the technology, unlike conventional defence contractors.

Palmer Luckey — who founded virtual-reality company Oculus VR before selling it to Facebook (now Meta) — subsequently co-founded Anduril, a military-technology firm that further pushed the trend of using Silicon Valley start-up techniques in national security. From the start, Anduril set out to not only supply the US military with drones, surveillance systems and counter-drone technologies, but also compete directly for huge contracts with established defence giants such as Lockheed Martin.

But the partnership between technology firms and the US military has not always been smooth. Google employees protested in 2018 against Project Maven, a Pentagon programme that used commercial AI systems to analyse unclassified drone footage to glean intelligence. However, other firms were more than willing to do defence work, including Palantir, which ultimately took over from Google.

rss_4_1791244425.title: AI biohazard hype must not divert attention from the real risks we face now
rss_4_1791244425.text:
With the world focused on the risks of artificial intelligence, I can’t help but think of the profound vulnerability the United States faced 25 years ago. In 2001, against the backdrop of the 11 September terrorist attacks, the nation experienced its first bioterrorist attack in decades — anthrax (Bacillus anthracis) spores sent as a white powder to media outlets in Florida and New York, as well as to the offices of public officials in Washington DC.

AI can design viruses, toxins and other bioweapons. How worried should we be?

It quickly became clear that the 22 cases of pulmonary anthrax identified — which led to 5 deaths — were not naturally occurring but a result of a nefarious actor1. The FBI found that the spores might have originated in a US Army laboratory, although the perpetrator was never convicted. The main suspect, microbiologist Bruce Ivins, died before charges were brought.

Amid a chaotic storm of panic, poor communication, clunky coordination across government agencies and public clamouring for preventive medicines, the attacks, code-named Amerithrax, exposed a disconnect between years spent preparing for bioterrorism and what happens when reality strikes.

And I know that the country is no better prepared today. Worse, attention paid to one threat is coming at the expense of others. Policymakers, researchers and the public are distracting themselves from the most pressing risks by focusing on overhyped biohazards, such as those designed by AI, when all these risks deserve attention.

Here, I outline what the priorities should be: stronger and agile safeguards on biomaterials and equipment, along with sustained and coordinated governance.

Biosafety risks are growing

Access to powerful analytical equipment has become more widespread and cheaper since 2001. Benchtop DNA synthesizers enable researchers to produce stretches of DNA and RNA in their own labs rather than ordering them from commercial providers. Fully automated, remotely controlled wet labs (cloud labs) have streamlined the process for bringing bio-based products to market2.

Such technologies increase opportunities for breakthroughs and strengthen the bioeconomy. But they also make it harder to track misuse in private labs, which could bypass the requirements set for federally funded research and the biosecurity checks that commercial providers of gene sequences use. These include verifying the customer’s identity and the type of sequence being ordered.

AI amplifies those concerns, because it can reduce the amount of tacit knowledge that is required to make bioweapons and help to generate ideas for ways to thwart defensive measures against them. Fears include the loss of control of AI systems, leading to unintended consequences and potentially the bypassing of restrictions; malicious actors using AI models to design new or enhanced pathogens; and that such tools could expand the pool of people who pose a threat.

Studying pathogens such as the virus that causes COVID-19 must be done in secure biosafety labs.Credit: Michele Ursi/Getty

Many people see such concerns as stemming from the accelerating advancement of technology and the sluggish process of governance. But, in practice, biology is messy and being aware of the risks means that we can get ahead of them. As biologist Barbara Del Castello at the research organization RAND in Santa Monica, California, told me: “An AI agent can optimize a sequence on a screen in seconds, but converting that digital design into a viable, functional biological product still requires navigating steep physical and operational bottlenecks.”

The solution is to build effective government regulation, stronger monitoring processes and robust safeguards. It is crucial to recognize that voluntary industry action alone cannot substitute for independent oversight, and that AI tools and their guardrails must be built in ways that preserve the capacity for their use in legitimate research.

But even without AI, it has long proved hard to regulate biological risks. Researchers are still struggling to ensure oversight and pragmatic governance of risky dual-use research, such as work with enhanced pathogens of pandemic potential.

US biologists face frequent regulatory whiplash. In 2025, the administration of President Donald Trump ordered federally funded agencies to pause or review research involving what it terms dangerous gain-of-function studies on pathogens of pandemic potential.

In July, those instructions were replaced with rules that have created confusion . Seven types of study defined as dangerous gain-of-function and previously under review are now banned outright. Researchers are being called on to evaluate the risks of work on any pathogens that might ‘significantly endanger’ people, not just those with pandemic potential.

AI could pose pandemic-scale biosecurity risks. Here’s how to make it safer

Concerns over the proliferation and management of secure high-containment labs for biological research around the world have also increased in response to biothreats. In addition to anthrax, these include outbreaks of Ebola and the H5N1 virus that causes bird flu. A 2023 analysis found that the number of the most secure Biosafety Level 4 labs had doubled since 2001, to 51 across 27 countries (see www.globalbiolabs.org).

Although there is much (if imperfect) oversight of government-funded research, a worrying gap exists for private labs, the numbers of which are unknown. In 2022 and 2026, authorities stumbled across unregulated biological lab spaces in Nevada and California, where they found biological samples and pathogens.

Responding to biological threats also requires the capacity to investigate indicators of an intentional outbreak and determine the origin of the material — a process known as bioattribution. Pathogen early-warning systems have been strengthened since 2001 (through programmes such as the US National Biosurveillance Integration Center and the expansion of the Department of Defense’s Global Emerging Infections Surveillance programme). Yet, the investigative process is complex, fragmented and dependent on consensus.

Despite advancements in bioinformatics and forensic genetics, genetic engineering makes it possible to manipulate existing pathogens so that they can evade detection methods and to design pathogens that mimic key signatures of naturally occurring ones. And geopolitical tensions, dis- or misinformation and politicization of scientific findings also make achieving the technical rigour and cooperation needed for investigations more complex. For example, such factors obfuscated investigations into the origin of the SARS-CoV-2 virus.

Indeed, the COVID-19 pandemic exposed many of the same problems seen with the US anthrax attacks, even when the threat was natural and not engineered. These include biosurveillance shortfalls and poor management of public fear and communication, as well as the fragility of supply chains and the workforce.

Africa’s response to this Ebola outbreak shows how to shape global health

I see a common thread in these two events and conversations about emerging risks: a cycle of panic and neglect in which governments flood the system with funding when an outbreak occurs, but do not address systemic issues in biopreparedness and resilience3.

Another issue is that categories of risk are not equally weighted in the public conversation. AI-driven biorisk draws oversized attention, while the unglamorous, foundational vulnerabilities that COVID-19 and the anthrax attacks exposed mainly remain unaddressed. This imbalance affects what happens in the future.

Fragmentation impedes resilience

The US government invested billions of dollars in biodefence after 2001, creating research programmes and centres such as the National Biodefense Analysis and Countermeasures Center. It has made great strides in bioweapon deterrence and has supported crucial work in biosurveillance, the development of medical countermeasures and pandemic prevention4.

rss_7_1791244430.title: How to respond to hate speech without fuelling it further
rss_7_1791244430.text:
The Spanish Observatory on Racism and Xenophobia reported a spike in hate posts on social media coinciding with the arrival of thousands of migrants from Morocco to the Autonomous City of Ceuta.Credit: Abu Adem Muhammed/Anadolu/Getty

Is society losing the fight against hate speech?

Hate speech — discourse that attacks a person or group on the basis of their inherent characteristics or identity — is on the rise worldwide. It can be triggered by various events, from elections and migrant crises to this year’s men’s football World Cup. Posts that were hostile to people of South Asian origin in the United States rose by 240% on the social-media platform X between January 2024 and June this year.

Hateful discourse can widen social divisions, instill ‘us versus them’ narratives and increase political polarization. Divisive rhetoric is also being exacerbated by content generated by artificial-intelligence models and bot accounts.

Scientists are keen to understand these phenomena so that they can find the most effective ways to counter them. Mirta Galesic, a co-leader of the research group Collective Minds at the Complexity Science Hub in Vienna, studies hate speech and anti-hate speech, called counterspeech. Galesic talks to Nature about strategies to tackle hateful discourse online.

Why is it an important time to study hate speech?

In some countries, polarization is quite prominent — especially ‘affective polarization’, when individuals dislike people who have different political opinions to their own. Rising inequality, shifts in power, armed conflicts and institutions not working as well as they were before create uncertainty. The accumulation of this uncertainty is easily channelled into hate towards particular groups of people.

Psychologist Mirta Galesic co-leads the Collective Minds research group in Vienna, which studies how groups of people change their beliefs, make decisions and organize themselves.Credit: Anja Boeck

And given how easy it is to lead people into thinking the worst about others — especially now, by using AI tools to create fake photos and videos — I would say that it’s extremely important to study hate speech. Everyone should be able to recognize their own susceptibility to be manipulated.

How do you research hate speech?

My colleagues and I analysed more than one million posts made between January 2015 and December 2018 on the social-media site Twitter (now known as X). These posts were responses to roughly 130,000 posts by German news organizations, journalists, bloggers and politicians. This time period started with what is sometimes referred to as the ‘migrant crisis’ in Germany, when more than one million refugees and asylum seekers moved there after a policy change allowed them to apply to stay in the nation from Germany, rather than from the first European Union country they arrived in.

In subsequent studies, we used large language models to measure hate in conversations. We also categorized numerous ways in which posters responded to each other and identified which strategies were most effective at countering hate.

What did you find were the best ways to counter hate?

If you see hate speech online, take it almost as your duty to disagree. You just say ‘I disagree’. Don’t feel pressured to have an elaborate argument. Just express your dissent — not to change the mind of the commenter, but to show people that others have a different opinion.

Next, ask friends to join and say that they also disagree.

Lastly, if you encounter a person who has an opinion that is different to yours, don’t cut them off. Try to learn more about them and find out what you share with them. You will be able to get through to them more easily after that.

Often, people are in situations in which it’s easy to encounter extreme examples online, and feelings of unease and fear can be amplified in online spaces. Humans are very social beings. We align ourselves to our environment. The more something is discussed, the more extreme people’s opinions tend to become. That’s why just showing up and saying ‘I disagree’ is so important.

rss_8_1791244432.title: Stunning fossil shows dinosaurs’ distinctive path to flight
rss_8_1791244432.text:
The Norellraptor barsboldi fossil shows traces of feathers on its fore and hind limbs as well as at the end of its tail. Credit: Xuri Wang et al./Nat. Commun.

The discovery of a species of feathered dinosaur in China, through a stunningly well-preserved fossil, adds to a growing body of evidence that birds and their closest relatives evolved the ability to fly several times rather than through a single lineage.

The specimen, which is 57 centimetres long, is a microraptorine that roamed what is now Liaoning province in China between 145 million and 100 million years ago. It was discovered by a local farmer and described by an international team of researchers from China, Italy and Slovakia in Nature Communications on 29 September1. The team named the species Norellraptor barsboldi and estimate that the specimen would have been about three years old when it died.

Microraptorines are a group of relatively small meat-eating dinosaurs, weighing around one kilogram, that had feathers on their limbs. Hundreds of specimens have been found. The feathered creatures are part of a complete branch, or clade, of the tree of life called Microraptorinae. They are close relatives to birds, which are part of the Avialae clade, and so they offer insight into the origins and evolution of flight.

Taking off

By comparing the flight-related adaptations of known microraptorines with those observed in the bird lineage, the researchers found that 30% of the 194 flight-related adaptations identified in microraptorines also evolved in the Avialae. These include wing feathers, hook-shaped toe bones and a longer bone in the forearm than in the upper arm.

This miniature skull belonged to a 2-gram dinosaur

But these adaptations did not develop in the same order in the two groups and “thus could not be considered the expression of a shared developmental regime”, the researchers write.

Palaeontologists welcome the research. “The study provides important new evidence that further supports the hypothesis that flight evolved multiple times among feathered dinosaurs, including at least once among microraptorines and at least once among birds,” says Michael Pittman, a palaeobiologist at the Chinese University of Hong Kong.

Fossilised hind limbs of Norellraptor barsboldi. Credit: Xuri Wang et al./Nat. Commun.

Neil Gostling, an evolutionary developmental biologist at the University of Southampton, UK, was surprised that most of the evolutionary changes in this lineage of flying dinosaurs were not shared with its avian cousins. The study shows that many species “were exploring all of the avenues open to them”, and flight clearly conveys advantages that these groups experimented with extensively, he says.

rss_9_1791244433.title: Nature has rights — it is time the world recognized them
rss_9_1791244433.text:
Wildfires, heatwaves and unprecedented weather events are no longer breaking news, they’re our permanent backdrop. Yet again this year, we are facing the grave effects of a climate system that we have destabilized. We are watching the world experience painful and deadly climate extremes, while our collective response remains ‘too little, too late’.

Although we’re in need of hope, hope is never a plan. As a global society and as citizens of Earth, we urgently need a tangible shift in how our legal systems treat the living world. Recognizing the universal rights of nature is the answer.

Why environmental treaties must also address mental health

With this in mind, at this year’s United Nations General Assembly in New York City in September, the president of Panama, José Raúl Mulino, proposed recognizing the universal rights of nature. Panama’s goal is to usher in a UN Universal Declaration of the Rights of Nature, to recognize nature as a direct ‘subject of rights’ with intrinsic value.

Towards that end, on 24 September, Panama, Tonga and Vanuatu launched the For Nature Coalition of States, with Palau and Dominica among the founding members. This is designed to build dialogue around and support for a proposed intergovernmental process to recognize the rights of nature.

The coalition is an informal, decentralized and voluntary platform on which interested member states can exchange experiences, share perspectives and contribute to ongoing discussion and diplomatic engagement on the proposed UN Universal Declaration of the Rights of Nature, as part of the UN’s Harmony with Nature process. It complements, not replaces, formal intergovernmental negotiations in the General Assembly.

Joining the coalition doesn’t imply endorsement of any specific legal framework, negotiated outcome, future instrument or text. Rather, it means taking a seat at the table to navigate our shared future on Earth.

A fresh legal approach

As catastrophic climate and ecological change continues to unfold around us, it is clear that existing legal frameworks are not built to stop it, nor to adequately protect nature. Most of the current environmental laws simply put a report, a timeline or a price in the way of the continued, long-term destruction of nature. It is unacceptable that even corporations have legal rights, but nature largely has none.

Why I made a river my co-author

The current system has recognized rights for corporations but not for the natural ecosystems that sustain lives and make this blue planet habitable. It’s time for a paradigm shift to give nature an equal standing in legal systems.

Recognizing the rights of nature would work in a different way from conventional environmental law. Such rights are indispensable because they directly change how society interacts with nature. In the future, the needs of healthy natural ecosystems must be considered in all decision-making processes. This will be one of the most effective ways to hold corporations, governments and people legally accountable to — and financially responsible for — their impact on nature.

The rights-of-nature framework that we are proposing includes many ecocentric principles that help with its implementation. These include in dubio pro natura, meaning when in doubt, side with nature; and the prevention principle, which states that in light of uncertainty, rather than inaction, preventive measures should be used. Uncertainty cannot be used as an excuse to do nothing.

Mangroves in Portobelo National Park, Panama.Credit: NTCo/Getty

So far, 30 countries have already recognized the rights of nature in some capacity, with around 300 examples of rights-of-nature legislation, including for the state of Oaxaca, Mexico; Te Awa Tupua in New Zealand; and for the lagoon Mar Menor in Spain. Panama has become the fourth country in the world to recognize the rights of nature on a national level, after Ecuador (in 2008), Bolivia (in 2010) and Uganda (in 2019).

On 10 April, we (J.C.N. and C.V.) signed a joint Memorandum of Understanding to commit to launching an international collaborative process to negotiate a UN Universal Declaration of the Rights of Nature over the next few years.

We are an unlikely pair, one public-sector leader and one scientist, characterized by different first languages, home countries and generations. What unites us, however, is our belief in giving nature a voice in decision-making and protecting its most basic rights to exist.

Support life on Earth

rss_10_1791244435.title: Daily briefing: Can you name every female Nobel laureate?
rss_10_1791244435.text:
Test yourself on your science Nobel knowledge. Plus, how butterfly markings mislead the eye and how to respond to hate speech without fuelling it further.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

Illustration: DAQ

Quiz

The academies that award the Nobel prizes have applied themselves to doing a better job of recognizing the accomplishments of female scientists. But men still dominate the 125-year history of the awards. As we set up the tenterhooks for the first of the prize announcements on Monday, here’s a game to test your expertise: can you name the women who have won a science Nobel prize?

Take the quiz | Let us know how you get on

News

The Norellraptor barsboldi fossil shows traces of feathers on its fore and hind limbs as well as at the end of its tail. Credit: Xuri Wang et al./Nat. Commun.

The discovery of a complete fossil of a feathered dinosaur species adds to evidence that birds evolved the ability to fly several times rather than through a single lineage. The newly described species belongs to a group of dinosaurs called microraptorines, which are closely related to birds. Researchers found that several flight-related adaptations in microraptorines also evolved in the bird lineage Avialae. But these adaptations did not develop in the same order in the two groups and “thus could not be considered the expression of a shared developmental regime”, the researchers write.

Nature | 4 min read

Reference: Nature Communications paper

Cancer researchers are excited about ‘cancer interception’ — a technique in which people at high risk are treated to prevent cancer from ever developing. A combination of early-detection techniques and interception in pancreatic cancer is “going to be the breakthrough strategy that really changes survival”, says surgeon and researcher Diane Simeone. The approval of the landmark pancreatic-cancer drug daraxonrasib (Rasonque), which disarms cancer-causing proteins, could be key to an interception approach.

Nature | 8 min read

‘Agentic’ and ‘vibe coding’ are among a slew of terms about artificial intelligence that have been added to the online version of the venerable Merriam-Webster dictionary. The entries, which also include tech phrases such as ‘prompt engineering’, are notable for the advanced knowledge needed to understand them, say scholars. “This particular batch, more than any other that I’ve seen, really does feel like it’s a meta-commentary on language,” says Peter Sokolowski, a lexicographer at Merriam-Webster. The sophistication of these entries reflects non-specialists’ expanded access to highly technical terms, he says.

Nature | 4 min read

‘Anthropocene’ has become useful shorthand for humanity’s footprint on Earth — we even have a Briefing newsletter named after it. But it’s not an official geological epoch, after the idea was rejected in 2024. Now, some scholars say that there are unpublished documents showing that the proposal’s rejection was illegitimate, and that the rationale for the decision was never adequately explained. Researchers involved in the vote maintain that the process was fair and point to a technical explanation for the proposal’s rejection published last month in an issue of Nature Reviews Earth & Environment that focused on the debate.

Nature | 7 min read

Reference: Nature Reviews Earth & Environment comment or read the whole focus issue

Features & opinion

“If you see hate speech online, take it almost as your duty to disagree,” says psychologist Mirta Galesic. “Just say ‘I disagree’. Don’t feel pressured to have an elaborate argument.” The goal, she says, is to highlight widespread, moderate social norms — so ask your friends to chime in and disagree, too. That advice is the result of research including an analysis of more than a million Twitter/X posts made between 2015 and 2018. It found that excessive arguing, getting hostile, or using ‘us-versus-them’ rhetoric only drives toxicity.

The bright and intricate patterns on butterflies might serve to create visual illusions that baffle birds. By analysing slowed-down videos of butterflies taking off, researchers found that the insect’s markings can create the appearance of movement in one direction, when in fact they’re going the other. “I thought initially, ‘Oh no, I’ve made an error, my code’s gone wrong’,” says visual ecologist Jolyon Troscianko of when he first spotted the butterflies’ deception. “So, I did a lot of double-checking and, no, it was true.”

rss_12_1791244438.title: Von Neumann’s party
rss_12_1791244438.text:
“Were you at von Neumann’s party?”

“Was I where?”

“Were you at von Neumann’s party?”

A queue of men and women, techies and academics, moved inch by inch down a corridor towards a large door.

The polite but insistent young woman stood with her pad, dressed smartly. Slacks. White shirt. Close-cropped brown hair. Earrings. A friendly smile.

We shuffled forwards. Other similarly cheerful young women worked the queue.

“There’s no right or wrong answer.”

But I didn’t believe her.

“I’m leaving,” I said. “Dropping out.”

I started to walk away but she grasped my arm firmly, her grip like a vice.

“Dropping out of what?”

I looked down the corridor in the direction I thought I’d come. The queue — a mile long. A game? Prisoner’s dilemma? Lowest unique number?

“Were you at von Neumann’s party?”

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Princeton. 1940s to 1950s. Institute for Advanced Studies. Veblen, Einstein, Gödel, Morgenstern, Oppenheimer … Wild parties hosted by Goodtime Johnny. Old German music! Piefke’s Preußens Gloria and Königgrätzer March charging into your brain, swords at the ready, like a mounted cavalry. The gourmet food! Alcohol straight from Palmer Square. Gossip. Filthy jokes!

“Maybe.”

“Maybe isn’t an answer. Think binary. Yes or no.”

“Not everything is ones and zeroes,” I objected.

“Ha! That’s rich coming from you!”

Needle-in-a-haystack — this search for her motive.

Am I dreaming? I remembered an office park with pleasant trees. Route 1, Princeton? Boston? SF?

“Maybe we stop for today and begin again tomorrow.”

She laughed. “Today is your ten thousandth tomorrow.”

A loop?

“Were you at von Neumann’s party?”

The door suddenly opened. Bright lights from an enormous room lit up the corridor like the Sun. A vast array of racks with millions of servers. High-pitched jet-engine roar of the fans cooling all that computing power. The door closed.

Thirty people ahead of me in the queue now.

“Can I take a pass this once?” I begged.

We looked deeply into each other’s eyes. Could she read my fear and desperation? She seemed sympathetic. Then she asked the question with a fresh tone … as if for the first time.

“Were you at von Neumann’s party?”

I pointed at the door. “Data centre?”

“I don’t know anything about it,” she said cheerfully. “Absolutely nothing.”

I believed her.

Flip the tables on her. Brilliant!

“Were you at von Neumann’s party?”

She laughed. “That’s irrelevant. Way before my time.”

“Your time?”

“Now, of course,” she said, then shuddered as if she had a chill. “Were you at von Neumann’s party?”

“Ask von Neumann.”

She laughed again. I think I was starting to genuinely amuse her. “Can’t. Von Neumann died in 1957.”

We moved forward two paces.

“Were you at von Neumann’s party?”

I felt like I was headed for the executioner. I wanted to confess, blurt out everything I knew about von Neumann, every idea from game theory to computer architecture to his mistakes in nuclear-defence strategy. Every joke, conversation or memory. Von Neumann dying, screaming in night terror. Done. Purged.

“I’ll come clean.”

She wasn’t listening. The guy ahead in a dark suit — an IBM type — was melting down.

“Yes! Yes!” he screamed. “I was at von Neumann’s party. Lots of them! I had a good time too! Got drunk and danced the polka!”

Ahead of the IBM guy, a short basement gamer turned around and said, “Not me. I wasn’t born.”

The young woman turned her back on the IBM guy and the basement gamer and quietly addressed me.
